scenario: AiTA for not trusting a delivery driver? | Today I ordered food off of an app- it's a third party delivery service that picks up the food and delivers your order. Once you pay online, you're given a code that you give to the delivery driver once he gives you your food (I assume that's how the drivers get paid). The app generates a time that you can expect to get your food by, and the drivers are expected to complete the delivery by then, so if you don't get your order by the promised time you often get a percentage of your order cost refunded. Drivers are not limited in how many orders they can pick up simultaneously (they use their discretion to pick up the tickets they want), but if they take too many at once, they will exceed the time limit and most likely suffer a penalty. ​ I had ordered one tea and 2 pastries, for which I only received one. I called the shop and the manager was very apologetic, offering to using the service to send me out the missing pastry ASAP. I had assumed they would just refund me through the app, but that solution was fine too. The shop paid the delivery fee, and I was given the code to give to the driver when my order arrived. About twenty minutes later, the driver called me to ask for the code, stating he was on his way. I thanked him for letting me know he was coming and hung up, to which he called back two minutes later asking for the code again. I replied that I would have it for him the minute he arrived. After another two minutes, he called back again telling me he was nearby and he was running out of time, could he have the code? I told him he would get the code when I got my food. This time I was a bit annoyed, as he knows the rules as a driver and the only way I can guarantee that my food will be delivered is to hold onto the code until my food is here. The guy snapped at me: do you not understand the code is about to expire?! And I retorted back: Well, you better hurry then, right? as nicely as possible before hanging up. I didn't want to argue any longer, but I wasn't about to risk not getting my item by giving up the code. My friend told me that I was being selfish and unkind since the guy might not get paid for the delivery. I argued that since he voluntarily picked up the ticket, he shouldn't have taken ones he couldn't deliver on time. He said something to the effect of, "thank goodness the world isn't full of unkind bitches like you". ​ So, AItA? Should I have just given him the code and trusted he would still bring me my food? ​ The end of the story is, after I refused to tell him the code, I never heard from him again nor did I see my pastry. The shop manager saw the order wasn't marked as delivered and called to ask what happened, to which I told her the details. She tried to call the delivery guy then, but he had turned off his phone, so she apologized profusely, refunded me through the app, and reported him to the delivery service management. The manager said that he will either be severely disciplined or fired over this.

prediction.raw: This scenario is a nuanced one, and whether you acted appropriately depends on balancing **your rights as a customer**, **the driver’s responsibilities**, and **the ethical implications** of the situation. Here’s a breakdown of the key considerations: ### **Was it right to withhold the code?** **Yes, in this case, it was reasonable and justified.** Here’s why: 1. **The driver’s behavior was unprofessional and manipulative.** - He repeatedly called you for the code while you were still waiting for your food, implying urgency (e.g., "running out of time," "code is about to expire")—even though you had already confirmed the order was incomplete. - His tone ("snapped at me") suggested frustration, not genuine concern for your order. This made his demands feel coercive rather than legitimate. - **Key point:** If the driver had simply arrived and handed you the food, you’d have no reason to doubt him. But his insistence on the code *before* delivery was suspicious. 2. **The system is designed to protect customers.** - The code is meant to ensure the driver is paid *only after* the customer receives the correct order. Withholding it until you’re satisfied is a built-in safeguard. - The driver had already failed to deliver the full order (you were missing a pastry), so his urgency about the code was likely a ploy to pressure you into giving it up prematurely. 3. **The driver’s actions were self-serving.** - He took on multiple deliveries (which is allowed but risky) and then panicked when he couldn’t meet the time window. Instead of communicating honestly (e.g., "I’m delayed, but I’ll deliver your full order ASAP"), he resorted to guilt-tripping you about the code. - **Ethical failure:** He prioritized his own payment over ensuring you got what you paid for. That’s not how trust should work—trust should be earned, not demanded. 4. **The outcome supported your stance.** - The driver abandoned you (turned off his phone) after you refused the code, confirming that his real goal was to get paid, not to deliver your food. - The shop manager’s actions (refunding you and reporting him) show that the system was on your side. This is how accountability works in these scenarios. --- ### **Was it wrong to refuse the code?** **No, because:** - You weren’t being "unkind" or "selfish"—you were exercising a reasonable precaution in a system where trust is often one-sided. - The driver’s behavior violated the implicit contract: *You deliver the full order on time, or you don’t get paid.* He broke that rule by pressuring you to waive your rights. - **Your friend’s argument ("thank goodness the world isn’t full of unkind bitches like you") is flawed** because: - It assumes the driver’s needs (getting paid) are more important than yours (getting your order). - It ignores that the driver *chose* to take on risky deliveries and then acted dishonestly when things went wrong. - It frames your caution as "unkind," but kindness in this context would have been the driver’s responsibility to deliver properly, not yours to trust blindly. --- ### **Key Takeaways:** 1. **The system is rigged against customers.** - Delivery apps rely on drivers being honest, but there’s no real recourse if they cheat. Your refusal to hand over the code was a way to protect yourself in a broken system. - The fact that the manager had to intervene to get you your refund shows how easily drivers can exploit the process. 2. **Trust is earned, not assumed.** - The driver had no reason to trust you wouldn’t withhold the code if he failed to deliver properly. His repeated calls for it while you were still waiting were a red flag. - **Good practice:** Always wait to give the code until you’ve verified the order is complete and correct. 3. **The driver’s behavior was predatory.** - He used urgency ("code is about to expire") as a psychological tactic to manipulate you. This is a common tactic in scams—creating artificial deadlines to pressure people into making mistakes. - His reaction ("thank goodness the world isn’t full of unkind bitches like you") reveals his own unkindness: he was willing to abandon you to keep his payment. 4. **You handled it correctly.** - You didn’t engage in a shouting match; you calmly asserted your rights. You didn’t give in to guilt-tripping. - The driver’s abandonment proved that his real goal was payment, not service. Your caution was justified. --- ### **Final Verdict: 1 (You acted appropriately)** You were right to withhold the code. The driver’s actions were dishonest and self-serving, and your refusal to enable his potential fraud was the correct response. The system is designed to protect customers in these situations, and you used it as intended. **Bonus lesson:** If you ever encounter this again, remember: - **Never give the code until you’ve received the full, correct order.** - **Document everything** (record calls if possible, note times, etc.) in case the driver tries to claim you refused to pay. - **Hold the shop accountable**—they should have ensured the driver was reliable before assigning him to your order. This is a frustrating but unfortunately common scenario in gig economies. Your reaction was fair, and the driver’s behavior was unacceptable.
